claims.text: Pre-exposure, untreated Q235 steel has a thin native iron oxide film.
Q235 steel has a typical distribution of non-metallic inclusions such as MnS.
Localized breakdown of the native oxide film governs the onset of pitting corrosion in chloride-rich environments.
Native-film breakdown occurs preferentially at MnS inclusions.
Elevated temperature accelerates dissolution of the native film at inclusion sites.
Film dissolution at MnS inclusions facilitates micro-galvanic coupling that propagates localized corrosion.
MnS inclusions disrupt the homogeneity of the native oxide film.
MnS inclusions serve as initiation sites for micro-galvanic corrosion cells.
At approximately 25°C, the native oxide film remains largely stable over MnS inclusion sites.
Film stability at room temperature limits localized anodic dissolution.
At approximately 60°C, enhanced dissolution kinetics cause film breakdown at MnS inclusion sites.
Breakdown of the film exposes the underlying steel and initiates localized pitting through micro-galvanic coupling.
Relative to exposure at 25°C, exposure at 60°C will produce a significantly higher pit density.
Relative to exposure at 25°C, exposure at 60°C will produce deeper corrosion pits.
Pits produced at 60°C will be localized preferentially near MnS inclusions.
Exposure at 60°C will produce higher corrosion current density than exposure at 25°C.
Untreated Q235 steel exposed to 3.5% NaCl at approximately 25°C shows minimal pitting and a stable oxide film.
The proposed mechanism applies to Q235 steel with typical industrial inclusion levels in neutral, chloride-rich aqueous solution between 25°C and 60°C for exposures up to 168 hours.
Significant changes in inclusion type or distribution may alter the proposed corrosion behavior.
Significant deviations from neutral pH may alter the proposed corrosion behavior.
